'''SQIsign''' is a [[Post-quantum cryptography|post-quantum]] [[signature scheme]] submitted to first round of the [[NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization|post-quantum standardisation]] process. It is based around a [[proof of knowledge]] of an [[elliptic curve]]{{efn|specifically [[supersingular elliptic curve]]s}} [[Endomorphism ring|endomorphism]] that can be transformed to a signature scheme using the [[Fiat–Shamir heuristic|Fiat–Shamir transform]].

It promises small key sizes between 64 and 128 bytes and small signature sizes between 177 and 335 bytes, which outperforms other post-quantum signature schemes that have a trade-off between signature and key sizes. SQIsign, however, has higher signing and verification times.<ref name="y877">{{cite web | last1=Westerbaan | first1=Bas | last2=Larisch | first2=James | last3=Ahmad | first3=Suleman | last4=Fayed | first4=Marwan | last5=Westerbaan | first5=Bas | last6=Valenta | first6=Luke | last7=Krivit | first7=Alex | title=Sizing Up Post-Quantum Signatures | website=The Cloudflare Blog | date=2021-11-08 | url=https://blog.cloudflare.com/sizing-up-post-quantum-signatures/ | access-date=2024-11-15}}</ref>
The original paper concluded that their [[C (programming language)|C]] implementation takes 0.6&nbsp;s for key generation, 2.5&nbsp;s for a sign operation and 0.05&nbsp;s or 50&nbsp;ms for a verification operation.<ref name="paper">{{cite journal | last1=Feo | first1=Luca De | last2=Kohel | first2=David | last3=Leroux | first3=Antonin | last4=Petit | first4=Christophe | last5=Wesolowski | first5=Benjamin | title=SQISign: compact post-quantum signatures from quaternions and isogenies | journal=Cryptology ePrint Archive | date=2020 | url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/1240 | access-date=2024-11-18 | page=}}</ref>

These times have been improved with new variations like SQIsign-east.<ref name="m912">{{cite journal | last1=Nakagawa | first1=Kohei | last2=Onuki | first2=Hiroshi | title=SQIsign2D-East: A New Signature Scheme Using 2-dimensional Isogenies | journal=Cryptology ePrint Archive | date=2024 | url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/771 | access-date=2024-11-15 | page=}}</ref>

The name stands for "Short Quaternion and Isogeny Signature" as it makes use of [[Isogeny|isogenies]] and [[quaternion]]s.

==Inner workings==
SQIsign is a [[Proof_of_knowledge#Sigma_protocols|sigma protocol]] for a [[proof of knowledge]] that is turned into a signature scheme using the Fiat-Shamir transform. The knowledge that is proven is an elliptic curve endomorphism.{{r|round2|p=5}}

SQIsign primarily operates on [[elliptic curve]]s. Two elliptic curves <math>E_1</math> and <math>E_2</math> can be connected with an isogeny <math>\varphi</math>, written as <math>\varphi : E_1 \rightarrow E_2</math>, which maps all elements of <math>E_1</math> onto <math>E_2</math>.
The fundamental problem that isogeny-based cryptography like SQIsign is based on is called the isogeny path problem and can be formulated as "find an isogeny <math>\varphi : E_1 \rightarrow E_2</math> given <math>E_1</math> and <math>E_2</math>", which is believed to be hard.
An endomorphism of an elliptic curve <math>E</math> is an isogeny that maps <math>E</math> onto itself, i.e. <math>\varphi : E \rightarrow E</math>.
The set of all endomophisms of an elliptic curve is known as its endomorphism [[Ring (mathematics)|ring]], written as <math>\textrm{End}(E)</math>.
The endomorphism problem can be formulated as "given <math>E</math>, find <math>\textrm{End}(E)</math>". Even computing a non-trivial part of <math>\textrm{End}(E)</math> is known to be as hard as computing the full <math>\textrm{End}(E)</math>.
This problem is known to be as hard as the isogeny path problem for supersingular curves like the ones SQIsign uses.
Furthermore, given two elliptic curves <math>E_1</math> and <math>E_2</math>, one can compute one of <math>(\textrm{End}(E_1), \textrm{End}(E_2), \varphi : E_1 \rightarrow E_2)</math> given the other two in [[Time_complexity#Polynomial_time|polynomial time]], i.e. the problem is easy.{{r|round2|p=5}}

The sigma protocol works as follows. The prover has <math>E_{pk}</math> and <math>\textrm{End}(E_{pk})</math> and publishes <math>E_{pk}</math> as their public key while keeping <math>\textrm{End}(E_{pk})</math> private. The prover then tries to convince the verifier that they know <math>\textrm{End}(E_{pk})</math>, which is hard to compute from just <math>E_{pk}</math> due to the endomorphism problem.{{r|round2|p=5}}<br/>
The protocol proceeds in 4 phases.<br/>
In phase 1, the prover commits to a random elliptic curve <math>E_{com}</math> and <math>\textrm{End}(E_{com})</math> and sends <math>E_{com}</math> to the verifier.{{r|round2|p=5}}<br/>
In the second phase, the verifier generates a random isogeny <math>\varphi_{chl} : E_{pk} \rightarrow E_{chl}</math> and its corresponding elliptic curve <math>E_{chl}</math>. Due to the isogeny path problem, it would be hard to compute the isogeny <math>\varphi : E_{pk} \rightarrow E_{chl}</math>.{{r|round2|p=5}}<br/>
In the third phase, the prover calculates <math>\textrm{End}(E_{chl})</math> from <math>\textrm{End}(E_{pk})</math> (i.e. their private key) and <math>\varphi_{chl} : E_{pk} \rightarrow E_{chl}</math>, since this problem is easy. They then calculate the isogeny <math>\varphi_{rsp} : E_{com} \rightarrow E_{chl}</math> that maps from the committed elliptic curve from phase 1 to the challenge elliptic curve from step 2. This can be done [[if and only if]] one knows the endomorphism ring of the prover's public key.{{r|round2|p=5}}<br/>
In the fourth phase, the verifier checks whether the isogeny truly maps from the committed elliptic curve to the challenge elliptic curve.{{r|round2|p=5}}

In order to make the sigma protocol secure, phase 4 has to be amended with a check that <math>\varphi_{chl}</math> is not a sub-isogeny of <math>\varphi_{rsp}</math> as an attacker could otherwise cheat and provide a forged isogeny without knowing at least part of the endomorphism ring.{{r|round2|p=6}}

SQIsign fixes the pair <math>(E_0, \textrm{End}(E_0))</math> and represents the private key as <math>\varphi_{sk} : E_0 \rightarrow E_{pk}</math> and the commitment as <math>\varphi_{com} : E_0 \rightarrow E_{com}</math> although this is computationally equivalent to the process described above.{{r|round2|p=6}}

The proof of knowledge protocol is transformed to a signature scheme using the Fiat-Shamir transform.{{r|round2|p=5}}

==Security==
SQIsign's security relies on the hardness of the endomorphism ring problem, which is currently considered hard.<ref name="f536">{{cite journal | last1=Page | first1=Aurel | last2=Wesolowski | first2=Benjamin | title=The supersingular Endomorphism Ring and One Endomorphism problems are equivalent | journal=Cryptology ePrint Archive | date=2023 | url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/1399 | access-date=2024-11-15 | page=| arxiv=2309.10432 }}</ref><ref name="l756">{{cite web | title=THE SUPERSINGULAR ENDOMORPHISM RING PROBLEM GIVEN ONE ENDOMORPHISM | url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/1448.pdf | access-date=2024-11-15}}</ref>

The authors also provide [[Nothing-up-my-sleeve number|a rationale for the chosen parameters]] in the last chapter of the specification.<ref name="spec" />

While SQIsign makes use of a similar construction, the weaknesses of [[SIDH]] do not translate to it.<ref name="spec" />

There is a security proof for SQIsign.<ref>{{cite journal | last=Aardal | first=Marius A. | last2=Basso | first2=Andrea | last3=Feo | first3=Luca De | last4=Patranabis | first4=Sikhar | last5=Wesolowski | first5=Benjamin | title=A Complete Security Proof of SQIsign | journal=Cryptology ePrint Archive | date=2025 | url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/379 | access-date=May 16, 2025 | page=}}</ref>

==Implementations==
There is a [https://github.com/SQISign/the-sqisign reference implementation] hosted on [[GitHub]].

==SQIsign 2.0==
The team behind SQIsign improved the original design in their round 2 submission and incorporated improvements from the SQIsign2D-West variant.<ref name=round2>{{cite web | title=SQIsign - Algorithm specifications and supporting documentation - Version 2.0 | url=https://sqisign.org/spec/sqisign-20250205.pdf | access-date=May 16, 2025}}</ref>

This has improved the signing time by a factor of 20 and the verification time by a factor of 6 while increasing the security level and reducing the signature size by 14%.{{r|round2|p=6}}

==Variants==
There are a couple of variants based on the original SQIsign:<ref name="page">{{cite web | title=SQIsign | website=SQIsign | date=2023-06-01 | url=https://sqisign.org/ | access-date=2024-11-17}}</ref>
* SQIsignHD: New dimensions in cryptography<ref name="m455">{{cite journal | last1=Dartois | first1=Pierrick | last2=Leroux | first2=Antonin | last3=Robert | first3=Damien | last4=Wesolowski | first4=Benjamin | title=SQISignHD: New Dimensions in Cryptography | journal=Cryptology ePrint Archive | date=2023 | url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/436 | access-date=2024-11-17 | page=}}</ref>
* SQIsign2D-West: The fast, the small, and the safer<ref name="q758">{{cite journal | last1=Basso | first1=Andrea | last2=Feo | first2=Luca De | last3=Dartois | first3=Pierrick | last4=Leroux | first4=Antonin | last5=Maino | first5=Luciano | last6=Pope | first6=Giacomo | last7=Robert | first7=Damien | last8=Wesolowski | first8=Benjamin | title=SQIsign2D-West: The Fast, the Small, and the Safer | journal=Cryptology ePrint Archive | date=2024 | url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/760 | access-date=2024-11-17 | page=}}</ref>
* SQIsign2D‑East: A new signature scheme using 2-dimensional isogenies<ref name="east">{{cite journal | last1=Nakagawa | first1=Kohei | last2=Onuki | first2=Hiroshi | title=SQIsign2D-East: A New Signature Scheme Using 2-dimensional Isogenies | journal=Cryptology ePrint Archive | date=2024 | url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/771 | access-date=2024-11-17 | page=}}</ref>
* SQIPrime: A dimension 2 variant of SQISignHD with non-smooth challenge isogenies<ref name="q029">{{cite journal | last1=Duparc | first1=Max | last2=Fouotsa | first2=Tako Boris | title=SQIPrime: A dimension 2 variant of SQISignHD with non-smooth challenge isogenies | journal=Cryptology ePrint Archive | date=2024 | url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/773 | access-date=2024-11-17 | page=}}</ref>
* SQIsign2D<sup>2</sup>: Improvement upon the SQIsign2D design.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Xu | first1=Zheng | last2=Lin | first2=Kaizhan | last3=Zhao | first3=Chang-An | last4=Ouyang | first4=Yi | title=SQIsign2D$^2$: New SQIsign2D Variant by Leveraging Power Smooth Isogenies in Dimension One | journal=Cryptology ePrint Archive | date=2025 | url=https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/920 | access-date=2025-09-03 | page=}}</ref>
